```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
pct <- function(x, d = 1) format(round(x, d), nsmall = d)
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

The more digested a prey item, the coarser the rank it can be named to. That
matters because digestion is not even across prey. Soft-bodied prey lose their
identifying features faster than fish with otoliths or crustaceans with hard
parts, so the material that can still be identified to species is a biased
sample of what was eaten. Buckland et al. (2017) asked diet studies to report
how prey condition affected identification. `dv_digestion_diagnostic()` gives
you that table.

The data are the public ICES stomach-content extract that ships with the
package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed
with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see `?ices_diet`), prepared as in
the getting-started vignette.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)
```

## A caveat on the stages

ICES records digestion as a code, 0, 1 or 2. The labels used here ("0
pristine", "1 affected", "2 skeletal remains") are inferred from the older ICES
format, whose three classes match the shares of these codes; they are not
taken from the ICES vocabulary. Read the stages as an ordered scale from fresh
to digested and check the labels against the ICES documentation before you
quote them. Records whose stage was not reported are kept as "not recorded".

## What the diagnostic computes

For every record, DietView finds the deepest rank with a name: its *finest
resolved rank*. Records with no name at any rank are "Unresolved". Within each
digestion stage it then reports the share of records, and of weight, at each
finest rank.

```{r diag}
diag <- dv_digestion_diagnostic(prep)
head(diag[, c("digestion", "finest_rank", "n_records", "p_records", "p_weight")], 7)
```

Side by side, the record shares are easier to read:

```{r wide}
round(xtabs(p_records ~ finest_rank + digestion, data = diag), 1)
n_stage <- tapply(diag$n_records, diag$digestion, sum)
n_stage
```

```{r diag-values, include = FALSE}
w <- xtabs(p_records ~ finest_rank + digestion, data = diag)
at <- function(rank, stage) pct(w[rank, stage])
gs <- function(stage) pct(w["Genus", stage] + w["Species", stage])
nr <- dat$digestion_label == "not recorded"
nr_dk <- sum(nr & dat$country == "DK")
```

Percentages are computed within each stage, so each stage adds up to 100%
whatever its sample size. Always read them next to `n_records`: here the
four columns hold `r paste(big(n_stage), collapse = ", ")` records respectively.

Pooled, the share named to genus or species changes little between stage 0
(`r gs("0 pristine")`%) and stage 1 (`r gs("1 affected")`%) and collapses at
stage 2 (`r gs("2 skeletal remains")`%), while the share named only to a
phylum or a class reaches
`r pct(w["Phylum", "2 skeletal remains"] + w["Class", "2 skeletal remains"])`%.
Stage 0 has its own oddity: `r at("Unresolved", "0 pristine")`% of its records
are unresolved, which a fresh prey should not be. These are unidentified
material recorded as undigested, a reminder that the stage describes the
record, not always the prey.

The "not recorded" column is not a fourth stage. `r big(nr_dk)` of its
`r big(sum(nr))` records come from Denmark, and `r at("Unresolved", "not recorded")`%
of them are unresolved. A missing stage follows the data provider, and
providers differ in how far they identify; dropping these records would not
remove them at random.

## Drawing it

```{r plot}
w_plot <- w[rowSums(w) > 0, ]            # no record stops at kingdom
cols <- c(grDevices::hcl.colors(nrow(w_plot) - 1, "Blues 3", rev = TRUE), "grey85")
barplot(w_plot, col = cols, xlim = c(0, 6.6), legend.text = TRUE,
        args.legend = list(x = "right", cex = 0.75, bty = "n"),
        names.arg = sub(" ", "\n", colnames(w_plot)),
        xlab = "Digestion stage", ylab = "% of records", cex.names = 0.75)
```

## Predator by predator

Pooled profiles mix predators that eat different prey and were sampled by
different countries. `by =` takes any column of the prepared data, including
the predator:

```{r by-predator}
top <- c("Atlantic cod", "Whiting", "European plaice", "Atlantic mackerel")
by_pred <- dv_digestion_diagnostic(prep, by = "predator_common")
by_pred <- by_pred[by_pred$by %in% top, ]
fine <- by_pred[by_pred$finest_rank %in% c("Genus", "Species"), ]
round(xtabs(p_records ~ by + digestion, data = fine), 1)   # % named to genus or species
xtabs(n_records ~ by + digestion, data = by_pred)          # records per cell
```

```{r pred-values, include = FALSE}
f <- xtabs(p_records ~ by + digestion, data = fine)
n <- xtabs(n_records ~ by + digestion, data = by_pred)
fp <- function(p, s) pct(f[p, s])
mack <- dat[dat$predator_common == "Atlantic mackerel", ]
mack_top <- sort(table(mack$prey_name), decreasing = TRUE)[1:4]
plaice_top <- names(sort(table(dat$prey_name[dat$predator_common == "European plaice"]),
                         decreasing = TRUE))[1:3]
```

- **Atlantic cod** shows the profile in its clearest form: the share named to
  genus or species falls from `r fp("Atlantic cod", "0 pristine")`% at stage 0
  to `r fp("Atlantic cod", "1 affected")`% at stage 1 and
  `r fp("Atlantic cod", "2 skeletal remains")`% at stage 2.
- **Whiting** starts lower, at `r fp("Whiting", "0 pristine")`%, holds at
  stage 1 (`r fp("Whiting", "1 affected")`%) and drops at stage 2
  (`r fp("Whiting", "2 skeletal remains")`%).
- **European plaice** has only `r n["European plaice", "0 pristine"]` records at
  stage 0, so its first column means nothing; at stages 1 and 2 it is
  `r fp("European plaice", "1 affected")`% and
  `r fp("European plaice", "2 skeletal remains")`%. Its three most
  frequent prey names, `r paste(plaice_top, collapse = ", ")`, are classes:
  much of what plaice eat is recorded at class whatever its stage.
- **Atlantic mackerel** is almost never identified to genus or species, at
  any stage. Its four most frequent prey names are
  `r paste0(names(mack_top), " (", mack_top, ")", collapse = ", ")`: the limit
  here is how the prey were recorded, not how digested they were, and most of
  its records have no stage at all
  (`r big(n["Atlantic mackerel", "not recorded"])` of `r big(sum(n["Atlantic mackerel", ]))`).

So the same stage does not mean the same identification depth in two
predators, and a pooled profile can hide both a steep and a flat one.

## How to read it

- If the species share falls steeply with digestion, as for cod, fine-rank
  results rest mostly on fresh material. Consider reporting them for the
  freshest stages separately, with the sample size you lose by doing so.
- Weight is affected twice: digested prey are both harder to name and lighter.
  A steep profile is a reason to be cautious with the weight currency in
  particular.
- Use `by =` with other strata too, for example `by = "country"`, when
  observers or protocols differ between them, or `by = "year"` when they
  changed over time.

The diagnostic describes identification; it does not correct for it. What
digestion does to the diet estimate itself cannot be measured on real data,
because the true diet is unknown. The vignette "A known diet" shows it on
simulated data where the truth is known: how much a diet description moves
when unidentified material is kept or dropped.

## Reference

Buckland, A., Baker, R., Loneragan, N., & Sheaves, M. (2017). Standardising fish
stomach content analysis: the importance of prey condition. *Fisheries Research*,
196, 126–140.
